verifyNotes: This review's assigned scope was a direct read of the article source (structure, the two required diagrams' markup, code-fence/formatting conventions, exercise forms) against docs/EDITORIAL_BRIEF.md, docs/WRITER_GUIDE.md and CONTENT_PLAN.md's design system section, not a live tools/verify-page.mjs run. No screenshots, Lighthouse numbers, console-error count or broken-link count were captured this round; lighthouse/consoleErrors/brokenLinks are left null rather than guessed, and should come from the consumer's serial verify-page.mjs pass per docs/ARTICLE_GAUNTLET.md step 5. Checks actually performed: grep for blank lines inside every block (none found, both diagrams clean); grep for literal fill="#..."/stroke="#..."/
justification:
Structure and flow are excellent and clearly the article's strongest axis. The single worked example (coin change for {1,4,5}) is carried, without a single break in vocabulary, through all nine `##` sections: brute-force recursion that measurably fails to notice repeated subproblems -> a diagram of that repetition -> a measured exponential blowup (10/20/30/40, doubling the amount multiplies the call count by ~3,200, not 2) -> memoization (with a find-the-bug exercise on a cache that is written but never read) -> tabulation with a fill-order diagram -> solution reconstruction -> space optimization to a 1D array (with a prove-it exercise that brute-force-checks the 2D and 1D tables agree for amounts 0..200) -> generalization to LCS and edit distance, both of which are explicitly tied back to the coin-change vocabulary ('the way `take` moved left along one row', 'walked backward from `dp[coins.Length, amount]`... exactly the way coin change's reconstruction walked backward') rather than restarting the explanation from zero -> a closing section that names the two CLRS properties (optimal substructure, overlapping subproblems) and extends the pattern to 0/1 knapsack without a full worked example, exactly as the plan's outline allows. No boilerplate Introduction/Conclusion headings; every `##` is specific to its content. Only `##` is used anywhere (confirmed by grep) -- a deliberately flat, non-nested structure that reads as a sequence of stages rather than a wall, matching the rhythm of sibling articles like recursion.md and greedy-algorithms.md. The three exercises (find-the-bug: a cache written but never read; prove-it: the two tables agree; extend-it: print the edit script) are well-formed, none is predict-the-output, and none leaks its output panel above the collapsed solution (confirmed: in each case the fence directly touching the exercise question has no `text output` block before `:::solution`). Two of the three exercise *labels* ('Find the bug', 'Extend it') are shared with recursion.md's exercise labels, but that is the site's own finite named vocabulary (predict-the-output/find-the-bug/extend-the-code/prove-it/measure-it) recurring across a 67-article plan, not a content repeat: recursion's find-the-bug is a swap-not-undone permutation bug and its two extend-it exercises are 'add memoization to Fib' and 'count directories'; this article's find-the-bug is a missing `cache.TryGetValue` check and its extend-it is printing an edit script from an already-built ops table. No two exercises share a scenario, a bug, or a program.

Code and readability formatting is very strong. Every fence uses a run-code.mjs-recognized tag (`csharp run id=...` throughout, `text output` immediately after each `run` block with nothing between but blank lines) -- confirmed both by inspection and by the absence of any fence irregularity. I measured every `text output` panel's longest line directly against the source: the worst case is 36 characters (the memoization block's `40: 114 calls, 40 computed  [...] ms`), and this holds for the LCS (`LCS: ATION`, 10 chars) and edit-distance/edit-script reconstruction outputs specifically named in this review's scope (`edit distance: 3`, 17 chars; the longest `sub   B -> G` line, 12 chars) -- the writer's self-reported ~40-column discipline holds everywhere, with margin to spare. Code-line width is nearly as clean: an automated scan of every fenced ```csharp block found only two lines over 85 columns, both at 87 -- two characters over the writer's self-reported reformatting threshold, not a large miss, but real. The more consequential of the two is `EditDistanceTable`'s final ternary branch (`: 1 + Math.Min(dp[i - 1, j - 1], Math.Min(dp[i - 1, j], dp[i, j - 1]));`, 16 spaces of indentation before it), which is exactly the line carrying the 'take the minimum of three neighbors' idea the surrounding prose spends a paragraph explaining; at the ~40 visible columns a phone shows, it clips inside the first `Math.Min(...)` call, before the nested one. This is not a lost fact -- the preceding paragraph already states the rule in words ('it considers substituting one character for the other... in addition to dropping a character from either side') -- but a reader scanning the code itself for the three-way comparison does not get it on a phone without scrolling, the same shape of issue this pillar has treated as minor before (see recursion.round-1.design.json's IL-inspection-output finding). The second 87-column line (the edit-script `'S'` branch inside the exercise solution) is lower priority: it is behind a collapsed solution, and its content (a `sub B -> G`-style line) is cosmetic string-building, not a formula a reader needs to read off the code.

Diagram quality is where this round falls short of a pass, and it is the reason the overall score sits at 7.6 rather than in line with the other two axes. Figure 1 (the `MinCoins(8)` recursion tree) is excellent: I recomputed the tree by hand from the article's own `MinCoins` (coins iterated in the order `[1, 4, 5]`) and every branch, every child ordering, and every highlighted node matches the code exactly -- root 8 branches to 7/4/3 in coin order, 7 branches to 6/3/2, 4 branches to only 3/0 (correctly omitting a coin-5 branch, since 5 > 4), and the three occurrences of remaining amount 3 are all correctly highlighted with `d-box-accent`. The figure is a real aid, not decoration -- it is the reason the 'overlapping subproblems' claim in the surrounding prose is verifiable at a glance rather than asserted. It is markup-clean too: viewBox 340 wide (under the 360 budget), no blank lines inside `<figure>`, no literal fill/stroke colors, unique ids, `<svg>` first child and `<figcaption>` last.

Figure 2 (the coin-change DP table) has a real bug. I reconstructed all three filled rows (i=1, i=2, i=3) by hand from `FillTable`'s recurrence and every printed value is correct (row i=3 is `0 1 2 3 1 1 2 3` for amounts 0-7, which matches `dp[3][j]` exactly). But the visual highlight does not point at the cell the figcaption and the arrow describe. The figcaption states 'dp[3][5], highlighted, is filled from dp[3][0] five columns to its left', and the curved arrow (`M56 84 C ... 210 84`) correctly ends near column 5's x-position (216), where the value `1` is rendered bold (`d-mono d-bold`, no accent color). But the actual colored/highlighted background rectangle in row i=3 -- the only visual element that reads as 'highlighted' the way `d-box-accent` reads everywhere else on the page (including col 0, which is correctly both accent-colored and bold) -- is placed at `x="168" width="32"`, which is column 4's position (168-200), not column 5's (200-232). A reader scanning the row for 'the highlighted cell' the caption promises will land on the accent-colored box at column 4 first, since it is the only other colored cell besides column 0 and is more prominent than a bold-but-uncolored digit one column over. This is not a cosmetic slip: `dp[3][4]` is actually filled by the *skip* path (`dp[2][4] = 1`, since coin 5 does not fit into amount 4) -- the row-above case the figure exists to contrast against the same-row `take` case -- so highlighting column 4's background actively illustrates the wrong mechanism at the wrong cell, one column away from the cell (column 5) whose same-row fill the figure and its caption are actually about.

issues.location: Figure 2 (id=cointable-title/cointable-desc), row i=3: the accent rect `<rect x="168" y="58" width="32" height="22" rx="3" class="d-box-accent"/>`
issues.problem: This accent (colored) background sits at column 4's position (x=168-200; column centers run 56, 88, 120, ... in steps of 32, so 168-200 is column 4, not 5). But the figcaption says 'dp[3][5], highlighted, is filled from dp[3][0]', the curved arrow ends near column 5's x-position (~210-216), and the bold (but not accent-colored) '1' text for the actual target cell sits at x=216, column 5. A reader looking for 'the highlighted cell' lands on column 4's colored box, one column away from the cell the caption, arrow and reconstructed value are describing. Worse, dp[3][4] is genuinely filled by the row-above 'skip' path (dp[2][4]=1, since coin 5 does not fit into amount 4), so a colored highlight there illustrates the opposite of what the figure exists to show (a same-row 'take' fill).
issues.fixLooksLike: Move the accent rect to `x="200" width="32"` so its background matches column 5, the cell the arrow and caption already point at, and give the col-5 '1' text a `d-text-accent` class (matching how column 0's accent cell pairs a colored background with `d-bold` text) so the highlighted cell reads consistently. Either remove the now-redundant plain-box split at x=200/width=96 (adjust to width=32 starting at 232 for columns 6-7) or otherwise stop drawing an accent box at column 4's position, since that cell is not the one being discussed and coloring it contradicts the row-above/same-row contrast the figure is making.

issues.location: `EditDistanceTable`'s final ternary branch, line ~545: `                : 1 + Math.Min(dp[i - 1, j - 1], Math.Min(dp[i - 1, j], dp[i, j - 1]));` (87 columns, 16 spaces of indentation)
issues.problem: An automated scan of every fenced csharp block found exactly two lines over 85 columns (both at 87), slightly past the writer's self-reported reformatting threshold. This one matters more: it is the line computing the 'minimum of three neighbors' that the edit-distance recurrence is built on, and at the ~40 visible columns a phone shows it clips inside the outer `Math.Min(...)` call, before the nested one is visible. The preceding paragraph states the rule in prose, so the fact is not lost, but a reader scanning the code itself for the three-way comparison does not get it on a phone without scrolling sideways.
issues.fixLooksLike: Break the computation so no single line carries all three neighbor lookups, e.g. `int best = Math.Min(dp[i - 1, j - 1], Math.Min(dp[i - 1, j], dp[i, j - 1]));` on its own line followed by `dp[i, j] = a[i - 1] == b[j - 1] ? dp[i - 1, j - 1] : 1 + best;` -- keeps every line under 85 columns and puts the operative `Math.Min` call within the mobile-visible window. The second 87-column line (the edit-script exercise's `'S'` branch, a string-building line behind a collapsed solution) is lower priority and can be left as-is or fixed the same round for consistency.

issues.location: Figure 2's `<defs>` block (the `cointable-arrow` marker, lines ~298-300), which appears after the `<path marker-end="url(#cointable-arrow)"/>` that references it (line ~297)
issues.problem: WRITER_GUIDE.md's copy-paste diagram template defines a marker in `<defs>` before any element uses it. This figure's marker is defined after its one use. Browsers resolve `url(#id)` marker references regardless of document order, so this does not break rendering, but it is inconsistent with the house convention and mildly harder to follow when reading the SVG source.
issues.fixLooksLike: Move the `<defs>...<marker id="cointable-arrow">...</marker></defs>` block to immediately after `<desc>`, before the first `<rect>`/`<path>` that uses it, matching Figure 1's own ordering in this same file (which has no `<defs>` block, so there is no internal inconsistency to point to there, but matching WRITER_GUIDE's template keeps every diagram in the pillar predictable to read).
